paragraphs.heading: Keeping secrets from listeners
paragraphs.text: Cryptography, also called cryptology, is the study and practice of ways to communicate safely while an adversary is trying to interfere. Put more broadly, it is about building and testing schemes that stop outsiders, or the public at large, from reading private messages. The word itself comes from two Greek parts, one meaning hidden and one meaning to write.

paragraphs.heading: Plaintext, ciphertext and keys
paragraphs.text: For most of its history, cryptography simply meant encryption: turning ordinary readable text, called plaintext, into scrambled nonsense, called ciphertext. Decryption is the same trip in reverse, from ciphertext back to plaintext. A cipher is the pair of procedures that do these two jobs. Each time a cipher is used, its exact behaviour is set by a key, a secret that is needed to turn the ciphertext back into readable text. A cipher without a changeable key is easy to break for anyone who knows which cipher was used.

paragraphs.heading: Alice, Bob and Eve
paragraphs.text: Writers in the field give the players stock names: Alice sends the message, Bob is meant to receive it, and Eve is the eavesdropper. The sender shares the way to decode only with the people it is meant for, to shut adversaries out. In everyday talk a code is any secret writing, but here it means swapping a whole word or phrase for a code word, so that wallaby might stand for attack at dawn. A cipher works below that level, changing single letters, syllables or pairs of letters.

paragraphs.heading: One shared key, or two keys
paragraphs.text: There are two main families of system. In a symmetric system, the only kind known until the 1970s, one secret key both locks and unlocks a message, and the work runs much faster. In an asymmetric system, a public key locks the message and a matching private key unlocks it. Because the public key can be published openly, two parties can start talking securely without first sharing a secret. In practice the asymmetric method is used to swap a secret key, and the conversation then continues with a quicker symmetric method. AES is a widely used, secure symmetric method.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to break, not impossible
paragraphs.text: Modern cryptography leans on mathematics and computer science. Its methods are built on assumptions that certain problems are very hard to compute, so a well-made system could be broken in theory but not in any practical way. Such systems are called computationally secure. Better methods for factoring whole numbers and faster computers mean these designs must keep being reviewed and adjusted. The one-time pad is different: it provably cannot be broken even with unlimited computing power, but it is much harder to use than the best breakable schemes.

paragraphs.heading: In daily life and in law
paragraphs.text: Cryptography is at work in online shopping, chip payment cards, digital currencies, computer passwords and military messages. Because it can serve spies and rebels, many governments have treated it as a weapon and limited or even banned its use and export. In some places where it is legal, investigators can be allowed by law to force someone to hand over the encryption keys for documents tied to a case.
